intro_html:
Both of Arizona’s 2026 plug-in bills died in committee, and a new one would have to be filed when the Legislature convenes in January 2027. Phoenix is split between APS, an investor-owned utility regulated by the Arizona Corporation Commission, and SRP, a public power district that sets its own rules. SRP’s FAQ addresses store-bought modular kits directly: “All systems, small or large, go through the SRP application and review process,” and all grid-tied equipment must carry UL certification.

Arizona’s solar-rights statutes are broad. A.R.S. §33-439 voids any covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract or other instrument affecting real property that “effectively prohibits” a solar energy device; §33-1816 bars planned-community associations from prohibiting one, allowing only placement rules that do not impair it or add to its cost; and §44-1761 defines the device to include systems serving on-site demand “at a residential dwelling unit or multifamily structure”. Read literally, that covers a balcony panel. But the statutes were written with rooftop systems in mind, we found no court decision applying them to a plug-in device, and they limit private restrictions, not the utility’s interconnection rules.

balco.nyc’s calculator models a specific Phoenix address and lets you enter the rate from your APS or SRP bill in place of Arizona’s 15.4¢ average.

faq: Can an Arizona HOA ban a balcony solar panel?

Arizona law is protective on paper. A.R.S. §33-1816 bars planned-community associations from prohibiting a solar energy device, §33-439 voids covenants in deeds and other real-property instruments that effectively prohibit one, and §44-1761 defines the device to include systems serving a residential unit or multifamily structure. We found no court decision applying these to a plug-in device, and they do not remove the utility’s interconnection requirement. This is not legal advice.
Does SRP allow self-installed small solar kits?

Only through its normal process. SRP’s FAQ, answering a question about installing a small system yourself, says all systems, small or large, go through the SRP application and review process, and that all grid-tied solar equipment must have UL certification.
